newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate panel delays vote on Pena nomination.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate panel delays vote on Pena nomination.

text.p: The Senate Energy Committee on Tuesday postponed a vote on President Clinton's nomination of Federico Pena to be U.S. Secretary of Energy, saying it wanted answers to new questions.

The panel also announced it had canceled action on a bill requiring the Clinton administration to build a temporary storage facility for spent fuel from commercial nuclear reactors. The White House opposes the measure.
The two votes had been scheduled for Wednesday, but would likely be considered Feb. 26, the committee said.
A Senate source said new questions were raised concerning Pena and would have to be answered before a vote on his nomination could go ahead.
But a White House official said it appeared the committee "might be holding up Pena's confirmation hearing in order to get the administration to back the nuclear storage."

The questions on Pena stemmed from a report in the Washington Times on Tuesday that said as Secretary of Transportation in 1994, he ordered Coast Guard contractors to rehire a minority business after it was terminated for poor performance.

Pena said in a letter Tuesday to Republican Sen. John McCain of Arizona that he was not acquainted with the company, DME Corp., and to the best of his knowledge had never met with its president or any other employee.
"These were the same questions raised two weeks ago and to which I have responded in writing ... I was advised that we responded fully to all questions," Pena wrote.

The vote on the nuclear waste bill, which utilities have pressed Congress to pass for the last two years, was postponed after a meeting on Tuesday between Senate leaders, President Clinton and Vice President Al Gore.

Republicans on the energy committee had the votes to pass the bill, which the administration threatened to veto, and planned to negotiate changes with the White House before the bill came up for a vote on the Senate floor, a Senate source said.
"They said they do not want interim storage at all," the source said, citing comments by Gore at the meeting.

Instead of trying to negotiate with the administration, the Republicans now planned to try to build a bipartisan coalition in the Senate in a bid to override the threatened White House veto, the source said.
